To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

high dose levels of a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (B[a] P) produced a G2 block in the epidermal cell cycle of the mouse, and a substantial inflammatory response in the skin, which together with the regenerative cell proliferation produced a marked epidermal cell killing.

the dose-response relationship between benzo[a]Pyrene (B[aP]) and the incidence of tumors was not correlated with the dose-response relationship for DNA adducts or for epidermal cell damage, as assessed by changes in cell kinetics and epidermal morphology.

the dose-dependent epidermal cytotoxicity and regenerative hyperplasia, and the inflammatory reaction in dermis associated with B[a]P treatment, were the likely basis of the tumor promotion activity of the agent.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a mouse skin model for studying the effects of chemicals on epidermal cell kinetics, and with the application of the model to studies of the effects of carcinogens and tumor promoters on epidermal cells in vivo.
the development of a quantitative model of the initiation-promotion stage of carcinogenesis in the mouse epidermis.
understanding the mechanisms by which environmental chemicals cause cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the high dose B[a]P treatment produced epidermal cytotoxicity and regenerative hyperproliferation, which was associated with a G2/M cell cycle block and inflammatory cell infiltration, and which was accompanied by the formation of DNA adducts, but which was not associated with epidermal hyperkeratosis, and which resulted in a dose-related increase in tumor formation.
B[a]Py acts as a tumor promoter in mouse epidermis, but that this activity is only evident in the presence of a tumor initiator.

B[a]Py is a tumor promoter at doses that produce extensive cytotoxicity, regenerative proliferation, G2/M cell cycle block, giant cells, pyknotic cells, dark cells, inflammatory responses and DNA adduct formation in mouse epidermis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the tumor-promoting action of B[a]p in this mouse model was associated with the induction of a high level of DNA adducts, a high level of cell killing, and a regenerative proliferative response, but not with a high level of epidermal hyperproliferation.
B[a]Pyrene is a complete carcinogen in the mouse skin model, but that the dose levels used in the present study reflect the action of a promoting agent.

B[a]Pyrene is a tumor promoter in mouse skin, that the dose-response curve for tumor promotion is different from that for tumor initiation and that the tumor promotion process is not dependent on DNA adduct formation in the epidermal basal cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
tumor promotion in this mouse skin model is associated with a high level of cytotoxicity and regenerative proliferation.
tumor promotion is not simply an increase in the incidence or multiplicity of benign tumors.
B[a]Pyrene is not a carcinogen in mice, but it is a tumor promoter in mice.
